chunks.heading: What makes an experiment random
chunks.body: A random experiment has more than one possible result, and you can't be sure which one will happen. Tossing a coin is a random experiment.
chunks.checkText: A random experiment is one where...

checkOptions.text: There is more than one possible result
There is only one possible result
The result is always the same

chunks.heading: Equally likely outcomes
chunks.body: Outcomes are equally likely when there's no reason to expect one more than another. Each face of a fair die is equally likely to land up.
chunks.checkText: Outcomes are equally likely when...

checkOptions.text: No outcome is more likely than another

chunks.heading: The basic probability formula
chunks.body: When outcomes are [[mathadv-equally-likely-outcomes|equally likely]], probability equals the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.

chunks.heading: The sample space
chunks.body: The sample space is the set of every possible outcome of an experiment. For a coin toss, the sample space is {heads, tails}.
chunks.checkText: The sample space of an experiment is...

checkOptions.text: The set of all possible outcomes

chunks.heading: The event space
chunks.body: An event space is the set of outcomes you're interested in, out of the whole [[mathadv-sample-space|sample space]]. Rolling an even number on a die gives the event space {2, 4, 6}.
chunks.checkText: An event space is...

checkOptions.text: A set of outcomes you care about

chunks.heading: Probabilities of 0 and 1
chunks.body: An impossible event has probability 0, and a certain event has probability 1. Every other probability sits somewhere between 0 and 1.
chunks.checkText: An event that is certain to happen has probability...

chunks.heading: The complement: probability of 'not'
chunks.body: The complement of an event is 'it does not happen'. P(not A) = 1 − P(A), since the two possibilities together cover everything.

chunks.heading: Estimating probability by experiment
chunks.body: Relative frequency is how often something actually happened, divided by how many trials you ran. Repeating an experiment many times gives a good estimate of its true probability.
chunks.checkText: Relative frequency is calculated by...

checkOptions.text: Dividing the count of an outcome by the number of trials

chunks.heading: Experiments with more than one stage
chunks.body: A multi-stage experiment has several steps, like tossing a coin then rolling a die. Each stage adds more possible outcomes to the [[mathadv-sample-space|sample space]].

chunks.heading: Graphing a two-stage sample space
chunks.body: For a two-stage experiment, you can plot every outcome as a dot on a grid, with one stage on each axis. This makes it easy to count outcomes for an event.

chunks.heading: Listing outcomes with a tree diagram
chunks.body: A tree diagram has a branch for each possible outcome at every stage. Following the branches from start to end lists every possible outcome of the experiment.
chunks.checkText: In a tree diagram, each branch represents...

checkOptions.text: A possible outcome at that stage

chunks.heading: What is a set
chunks.body: A set is just a collection of things, called its members. We can write a set by listing its members inside curly brackets, like {1, 3, 5}.
chunks.checkText: The members of a set are listed inside...

chunks.heading: Counting the members of a set
chunks.body: The size of a [[mathadv-sets-intro|set]] S is written |S|, and just means how many members it has. If S = {2, 4, 6}, then |S| = 3.
chunks.checkText: |S| means...

checkOptions.text: The number of members in set S
The sum of the members of S

chunks.heading: Intersection: 'and'
chunks.body: The intersection of two sets, written A∩B, contains only the members that are in both sets. It's what mathematicians mean by 'and'.
chunks.checkText: A∩B contains members that are...

checkOptions.text: In A or B, or both

chunks.heading: Union: 'or'
chunks.body: The union of two sets, written A∪B, contains every member that's in A, in B, or in both. It's what mathematicians mean by 'or'.
chunks.checkText: A∪B contains members that are...

checkOptions.text: In A, in B, or in both
Only in both A and B

chunks.heading: Disjoint sets
chunks.body: Two sets are disjoint if they share no members at all, so their [[mathadv-intersection|intersection]] is empty. {1, 2} and {3, 4} are disjoint.
chunks.checkText: Two sets are disjoint when...

checkOptions.text: They have no members in common
They have every member in common
One set is bigger than the other

chunks.heading: Venn diagrams
chunks.body: A Venn diagram uses overlapping circles inside a rectangle to show how sets relate. The overlap shows the [[mathadv-intersection|intersection]] of the sets.
chunks.checkText: In a Venn diagram, the overlapping region between two circles shows...

checkOptions.text: The intersection of the two sets
The union of the two sets

chunks.heading: Complement of a set: 'not'
chunks.body: The complement of a set A, written Ā, is everything outside A but still within the universal set. It's what mathematicians mean by 'not'.

chunks.heading: The counting rule for two sets
chunks.body: To count the union of two sets, add their sizes then subtract the size of their [[mathadv-intersection|intersection]], so shared members aren't double-counted: |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B|.

checkOptions.text: Because those members were counted twice
To make the union smaller than A

chunks.heading: Mutually exclusive events
chunks.body: Two events are mutually exclusive if they can never both happen at once. Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on the same die throw are mutually exclusive.
chunks.checkText: Mutually exclusive events are events that...

checkOptions.text: Cannot both occur at the same time

chunks.heading: Adding probabilities of exclusive events
chunks.body: For [[mathadv-mutually-exclusive-events|mutually exclusive]] events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), since there's no overlap to worry about.

chunks.heading: The general addition rule
chunks.body: When events can overlap, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B), so the overlap isn't counted twice. This matches the [[mathadv-counting-rule|counting rule]] for sets.

chunks.heading: Independent events
chunks.body: Two events are independent if one happening doesn't change the chance of the other happening. Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent of each other.
chunks.checkText: Two events are independent when...

checkOptions.text: One doesn't affect the probability of the other

chunks.heading: Multiplying probabilities: the product rule
chunks.body: For two [[mathadv-independent-events-intro|independent]] stages, multiply their probabilities together: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

chunks.heading: The product rule for many stages
chunks.body: The [[mathadv-product-rule-two-stage|product rule]] extends to any number of independent stages. Just multiply the probability of each stage together.

chunks.heading: Sampling without replacement
chunks.body: When an item isn't put back before the next draw, the probabilities for later draws change. Drawing two marbles without replacing the first is an example.

checkOptions.text: Removed items are not returned before the next draw
Only one item is ever drawn

chunks.heading: Building a probability tree diagram
chunks.body: A probability tree diagram writes the probability on each branch. Multiply along a path to get that outcome's probability, then add outcomes that match what you want.
chunks.checkText: In a probability tree diagram, you multiply along the branches to find...

checkOptions.text: The probability of one full path of outcomes

chunks.heading: Conditional probability: new information changes things
chunks.body: Conditional probability is the chance of an event once you know something else has already happened. Knowing a die roll is even changes the chance it was a 6.
chunks.checkText: Conditional probability is used when...

checkOptions.text: New information changes the sample space
No information is available at all

chunks.heading: The formula for conditional probability
chunks.body: P(A|B) means the probability of A given that B has happened. It's calculated as P(A|B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).

chunks.heading: Testing for independence
chunks.body: Events A and B are independent exactly when P(A|B) = P(A), meaning knowing B happened doesn't change A's probability. This matches the [[mathadv-conditional-probability-formula|conditional probability]] idea.

chunks.heading: What is a probability distribution
chunks.body: A probability distribution lists every possible outcome of an experiment together with its probability. All the probabilities in the list add up to 1.
chunks.checkText: The probabilities in a probability distribution always add up to...

chunks.heading: The random variable X
chunks.body: A random variable, usually called X, stands for the numeric result of a random experiment. X might be the number of heads when you toss three coins.
chunks.checkText: A random variable represents...

checkOptions.text: The numeric result of a random experiment

chunks.heading: Numeric and categorical data
chunks.body: Numeric data are values you can do maths with, like a count of heads. Categorical data are labels, like the colour of a marble drawn from a bag.
chunks.checkText: The colour of a ball drawn from a bag is an example of...

chunks.heading: Uniform probability distributions
chunks.body: A distribution is uniform when every outcome has exactly the same probability. Rolling a fair die gives a uniform distribution, since each number has probability 1/6.
chunks.checkText: A distribution is uniform when...

checkOptions.text: Every outcome has the same probability

chunks.heading: The notation p(x)
chunks.body: p(x) is short for P(X = x), the probability that the [[mathadv-random-variable|random variable]] X takes the value x. It's just a quicker way to write the same thing.
chunks.checkText: p(x) means the same thing as...

chunks.heading: What expected value means
chunks.body: Expected value is the long-run average result if you repeated an experiment many, many times. It's also called the mean of the distribution.
chunks.checkText: Expected value describes...

checkOptions.text: The long-run average result of an experiment

chunks.heading: The formula for expected value
chunks.body: Expected value is found by multiplying each outcome by its probability, then adding up all the results: E(X) = Σ x p(x).
chunks.checkText: To find E(X), for each outcome you...

checkOptions.text: Multiply the value by its probability, then add them all
Just add up all the values

chunks.heading: Calculating expected value in a table
chunks.body: A handy way to find [[mathadv-expected-value-formula|expected value]] is to add a row to the distribution table showing x times p(x), then sum that row.

checkOptions.text: x multiplied by p(x) for each outcome
x divided by p(x) for each outcome

chunks.heading: How far a value is from the mean
chunks.body: The deviation of a value x is how far it sits from the mean μ, written x − μ. Values above the mean have a positive deviation, and values below have a negative one.

chunks.heading: Variance: measuring spread
chunks.body: Variance measures how spread out a distribution's values are from the mean. It's the weighted average of the squared [[mathadv-deviation-from-mean|deviations]]: Var(X) = Σ(x − μ)² p(x).
chunks.checkText: Variance measures...

checkOptions.text: How spread out the values are from the mean

chunks.heading: A quicker way to calculate variance
chunks.body: An easier formula gives the same answer: Var(X) = E(X²) − μ², where E(X²) is found by summing x² p(x). This avoids working with fraction means.

chunks.heading: Standard deviation
chunks.body: Standard deviation is the square root of the [[mathadv-variance-definition|variance]]. Unlike variance, it's measured in the same units as the original values.
chunks.checkText: Standard deviation is found by...

checkOptions.text: Taking the square root of the variance
Dividing the variance by the mean

chunks.heading: Sample versus population
chunks.body: A population is every possible result of an experiment, while a sample is just the results you actually collected by running it several times.
chunks.checkText: A sample, compared to a population, is...

checkOptions.text: Just some of the results, actually collected
Every possible result there could be

chunks.heading: The sample mean
chunks.body: The sample mean, written x̄, is the average of the values you actually collected. It's found the same way as [[mathadv-expected-value-formula|expected value]], but using relative frequencies instead of true probabilities.
chunks.checkText: The sample mean x̄ is calculated from...

checkOptions.text: The relative frequencies of the collected results

chunks.heading: Sample variance and standard deviation
chunks.body: Sample variance s² and sample standard deviation s measure spread in a collected sample, just like [[mathadv-variance-definition|variance]] and [[mathadv-standard-deviation|standard deviation]] do for a full distribution.

chunks.heading: Census versus survey
chunks.body: A census asks everyone in a population, while a survey only asks some of them. Surveys are usually quicker and cheaper, but a census gives exact results.
